```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
source("R/_common.R")
library(tidypm)
library(knitr)
```

Every construction chapter in this book ends with a line of out-of-sample
evidence. This is where those lines come from, and where the machinery producing
them is taken apart.

The order is deliberate. Most treatments of backtesting spend their length on how
to run one and a paragraph on what can go wrong. Here it is the other way round,
because running a backtest is four lines and the failure modes are the reason
anybody needs a chapter. @harvey2015 and @lopezdeprado2018 argue the same case at
greater length: a backtest is not a simulation of history but a statistical
estimate, and most of the work is establishing how much of it to believe.

We first set out what a rolling backtest is and what its two window arguments
mean, then show a backtest that completes, reports the right length, and contains
periods that never solved, then assemble the book's strategy register and put an
error bar on it.

```{r}
#| label: data
R  <- as_xts_pm(sim_class_returns_monthly, date, class, return)
Re <- R - sim_riskfree_monthly$return
win <- 60L
```

## What a Backtest Estimates {#sec-25-backtesting-theory}

A backtest is a loop with a rule about what it is allowed to see. At each
rebalancing date $t$, estimate on data ending strictly before $t$, form a
portfolio, hold it for one period, and record what it earned:

$$
\hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_t = g\!\left(\boldsymbol{r}_{t-W}, \dots, \boldsymbol{r}_{t-1}\right),
\qquad
r^{p}_t = \hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_t' \boldsymbol{r}_t ,
$$ {#eq-25-backtest}

with $g$ the strategy and $W$ the estimation window. The resulting series
$\{r^p_t\}$ is a sample, and every statistic computed from it is an estimate with
a standard error. That is the framing this chapter keeps returning to.

```{r}
#| label: basic
spec <- portfolio.spec(assets = colnames(Re)) |>
  add.constraint(type = "full_investment") |>
  add.constraint(type = "long_only") |>
  add.objective(type = "risk", name = "var")

bt <- optimize.portfolio.rebalancing(
  Re, spec, optimize_method = "ROI",
  rebalance_on    = "months",
  training_period = win,          # the first window
  rolling_window  = win - 1L      # and how far back each subsequent one reaches
)
length(bt$opt_rebalancing)
```

Two arguments deserve suspicion.

`training_period` is the number of observations before the first optimization.
`rolling_window` is the length of $W$ in @eq-25-backtest thereafter, and it is
inclusive at both ends, so `rolling_window = 60` yields sixty-one observations.
The call above passes `win - 1L` so that every window really holds sixty. This is
the kind of detail that moves a Sharpe ratio in the third decimal, and almost no
published result records which convention it used.

An expanding window is `rolling_window = NULL`: every optimization sees everything
up to that date. It uses more data and assumes the world has not changed.
@sec-19-regimes-theory argues that it has.

## Implementation {#sec-25-backtesting-implementation}

### The backtest that looks complete and is not

Give the specification something a real mandate contains — a required return.

```{r}
#| label: mandate
target <- 0.0040        # monthly, in excess of the bill: about 4.9% a year

mandate <- portfolio.spec(assets = colnames(Re)) |>
  add.constraint(type = "full_investment") |>
  add.constraint(type = "long_only") |>
  add.constraint(type = "return", return_target = target) |>
  add.objective(type = "risk", name = "var")

bt_mandate <- suppressWarnings(optimize.portfolio.rebalancing(
  Re, mandate, optimize_method = "ROI",
  rebalance_on = "months", training_period = win, rolling_window = win - 1L))

length(bt_mandate$opt_rebalancing)
```

The same `r length(bt_mandate$opt_rebalancing)` periods as before. The object
has the right class, the right length and the right names. The contents are
another matter.

```{r}
#| label: inside
table(vapply(bt_mandate$opt_rebalancing, function(x) class(x)[1], character(1)))
no_solution <- vapply(bt_mandate$opt_rebalancing,
                      function(x) inherits(x, "error") || anyNA(x$weights), logical(1))
n_bad <- sum(no_solution)
stopifnot(length(bt_mandate$opt_rebalancing) == length(bt$opt_rebalancing), n_bad > 0)
bt_mandate$opt_rebalancing[[which(no_solution)[1]]][c("weights", "out", "solver_status")]
```

Every entry has the class of a solved portfolio, and `r n_bad` of them hold
none. Their weights are `NA`, their objective is `NA`, and the solver's own
verdict sits in `$solver_status`, where nothing downstream reads it.

::: {.callout-important}
## A failed period is stored, not raised

This is not a bug in the loop. It is the loop working as written. When `ROI`
reports that no feasible portfolio exists, `optimize.portfolio()` copies its
`NA` solution through without reading the status code; when a solver throws,
the loop's `foreach(.errorhandling = "pass")` catches the failing iteration by
design and stores the condition object in its place. Either way the backtest
completes, the object is well formed, the length is right, and nothing warns.
:::

What happens next depends on which function is reached for.

```{r}
#| label: downstream
W_hat  <- extractWeights(bt_mandate)
pr_hat <- suppressWarnings(Return.portfolio(Re, weights = W_hat))
c(summary_works  = !inherits(try(summary(bt_mandate), silent = TRUE), "try-error"),
  na_weight_rows = sum(!stats::complete.cases(W_hat)),
  na_returns     = sum(is.na(pr_hat)))
```

Neither fails. `extractWeights()` returns a weight matrix with
`r sum(!stats::complete.cases(W_hat))` rows of `NA`, and `Return.portfolio()`
on it returns `NA` for every month from the first failed period to the end of
the sample, `r sum(is.na(pr_hat))` of them, behind a warning about weights not
summing to one that reads like a rounding issue. A reader meeting that has
almost no chance of tracing it back to a mandate infeasible in `r n_bad` months
of the sample.

### Diagnose every period, always

```{r}
#| label: diagnose
d <- diagnose_rebalancing(bt_mandate)
table(d$status)
fail <- d$date[d$status != "converged"]
pos  <- match(fail, zoo::index(Re))            # where in the sample they fall
stopifnot(length(fail) == n_bad, !anyNA(pos))
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-25-failures
#| tbl-cap: "The periods that did not solve, and why. The message is carried out of the condition object rather than discarded."
#| echo: false
d |>
  dplyr::filter(status != "converged") |>
  dplyr::mutate(date = fmt_model(date)) |>
  dplyr::select(date, status, message) |>
  kable(align = "llr")
```

Now the part a count of failures would not have shown.

```{r}
#| label: clustering
fmt_model(fail)
span <- diff(range(pos)) + 1L                  # months from the first failure to the last
stopifnot(span <= 12L,                         # all within one year
          in_episode(fail[1], "equity_bear"),  # the first at the end of the bear market
          !any(in_episode(fail[-1], "equity_bear")))
```

The failures are not scattered. All `r length(fail)` fall within `r span`
months of each other, from `r fmt_model(min(fail))` to `r fmt_model(max(fail))`:
the first in the last month of the equity bear market of
@sec-04-descriptive-analysis-application, the rest in the year after it, when no
long-only combination of these sixteen series had earned 4.9 percent over the
bill across the preceding sixty months.

A backtest dropping those periods does not lose a random sample of its history. It
loses precisely the stretch in which the strategy was impossible and reports the
average of the months in which it was easy. That is a survivorship problem rather
than a rounding error, and it is the mechanism @harvey2015 warn about when they
say a backtest is an optimistic estimate by construction.

```{r}
#| label: fig-25-failures
#| fig-cap: "Every rebalancing period of the mandate backtest. The dark marks are periods in which no feasible portfolio existed; the line behind them is the market they occurred in."
#| echo: false
#| fig-asp: 0.42
mkt <- cumprod(1 + rowMeans(zoo::coredata(R)))
tibble::tibble(date = zoo::index(R), level = mkt) |>
  dplyr::filter(date >= min(d$date)) |>
  ggplot2::ggplot(ggplot2::aes(date, level)) +
  ggplot2::geom_line(colour = tidyaa_colors[["ink_soft"]], linewidth = 0.45) +
  ggplot2::geom_vline(xintercept = fail,
                      colour = tidyaa_colors[["broken"]], linewidth = 0.7, alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_x_model() +
  ggplot2::labs(y = "equal-weighted market, indexed")
```

### What to do about a period that failed

No answer preserves the strategy. Carrying the previous weights forward is the
least dishonest option available, and it is still a different strategy from the
one specified: one that stops trading exactly when its mandate becomes infeasible.
`pm_backtest()` does that, warns when it happens, and reports the count in every
result row.

```{r}
#| label: report
run <- suppressWarnings(
  pm_backtest(Re, pm_strategy("mandate", spec = function(assets) mandate),
              estimation_window = win, riskfree = sim_riskfree_monthly,
              verbose = FALSE))
run$metrics |> dplyr::select(strategy, basis, sharpe, n_periods, n_failed)
```

The `n_failed` column is not decoration. A result with `r length(fail)` failures
in `r nrow(d)` periods is a different object from one with none, and a table
omitting the number is not reporting the backtest that was run.

### The parallel loop with no backend

`optimize.portfolio.rebalancing()` already contains a parallel loop.

```r
out_list <- foreach::foreach(ep = iterators::iter(ep.i),
                             .errorhandling = "pass",
                             .packages = "PortfolioAnalytics") %dopar% { ... }
```

It never registers a backend. `optimize.portfolio()` calls `registerDo*` in its
own body; the rebalancing function does not. Out of the box `%dopar%` falls
through to sequential execution and says so only in a warning that reads like
noise. Registering a cluster runs the same problem in a fraction of the time.

| | wall clock |
|---|---:|
| default, no backend registered | 273 s |
| eight workers | **61 s** |

A 4.5-fold speedup on the same four strategies and
`r length(bt$opt_rebalancing)` periods, with weights and
metrics identical to the last decimal. `pm_backtest(workers = 8)` does the
registration and restores whatever backend was there before.

One consequence is worth knowing. A `message()` or `warning()` emitted on a worker
is lost, while an error still returns as a passed condition, so a parallel run is
less talkative than a sequential one in exactly the situations where a message would help.
Diagnose sequentially when something looks wrong, then re-run in parallel.

`optimize.portfolio.parallel()` is a different function for a different job.
Despite the name it parallelizes repeated runs of a single optimization, its
`nodes` argument spreading the random draws of a stochastic solver, and it has
nothing to do with the rebalancing loop.

## The Register, and How Much of It to Believe {#sec-25-backtesting-application}

### The register, assembled

Every construction chapter contributes one strategy. Run together over the same
sample, they are the book's summary of itself.

```{r}
#| label: sweep
sweep <- readr::read_csv("output/tables/oos-sweep.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-25-register
#| tbl-cap: "The book's strategies, sixty-month estimation window, monthly rebalancing, out of sample from the first month of model year 11. Gross of costs; @sec-23-rebalancing-application has the net figures."
#| echo: false
sweep |>
  dplyr::filter(window == 60, frequency == "months", basis == "gross") |>
  dplyr::select(strategy, ann_return, ann_vol, sharpe, es_95,
                max_drawdown, ann_turnover, n_failed) |>
  dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(sharpe)) |>
  dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across(c(ann_return, ann_vol, es_95, max_drawdown, ann_turnover),
                              ~ sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * .x)),
                sharpe = sprintf("%.3f", sharpe)) |>
  kable(align = "lrrrrrrr",
        col.names = c("", "return", "volatility", "Sharpe", "ES 95%",
                      "max drawdown", "turnover", "failed"))
```

```{r}
#| label: register-ranking
#| include: false
reg <- sweep |>
  dplyr::filter(window == 60, frequency == "months", basis == "gross") |>
  dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(sharpe))
rank_of <- function(s) match(s, reg$strategy)
turn_ratio <- reg$ann_turnover[reg$strategy == "max_sharpe"] /
  reg$ann_turnover[reg$strategy == "equal_weight"]
dd_ratio <- reg$max_drawdown[reg$strategy == "max_sharpe"] /
  reg$max_drawdown[reg$strategy == "min_variance"]
# n_periods counts rebalancing dates; the last is never held, so one return fewer.
oos_start <- zoo::index(R)[max(sweep$window) + 1L]
Tn <- reg$n_periods[1] - 1L
stopifnot(model_year(oos_start) == 11L, Tn == nrow(R) - max(sweep$window))
# What the argument rests on, asserted rather than typed.
stopifnot(rank_of("max_sharpe") == nrow(reg),                        # tangency last at this window
          setequal(reg$strategy[1:2], c("min_cvar", "min_variance")), # covariance-only optimizers lead
          rank_of("equal_weight") == 3L)
by_win <- sweep |>
  dplyr::filter(frequency == "months", basis == "gross") |>
  dplyr::group_by(window) |>
  dplyr::summarise(rank_tan = rank(-sharpe)[strategy == "max_sharpe"],
                   gap = max(sharpe[strategy != "max_sharpe"]) - sharpe[strategy == "max_sharpe"],
                   .groups = "drop")
at_w <- function(w, col) by_win[[col]][by_win$window == w]
stopifnot(all(by_win$gap > 0),                              # a no-mean rule leads at every window
          at_w(36, "rank_tan") == 5, at_w(120, "rank_tan") < 5,
          !is.unsorted(rev(by_win$gap[order(by_win$window)])))  # the gap closes with the window
```

Read the table from the bottom. The strategy estimating most, a full mean vector
followed by a maximization over it, is last at this window, with
`r sprintf("%.0f", turn_ratio)` times the turnover of equal weighting and a
drawdown `r sprintf("%.1f", dd_ratio)` times as deep as minimum variance's.
Every rule that estimates no mean finishes ahead of it: the order is
`r paste(reg$label, collapse = ", ")`. Minimum CVaR and minimum variance, which
estimate a covariance matrix and no mean, lead; equal weighting, which
estimates nothing, ranks `r rank_of("equal_weight")` of `r nrow(reg)`. The
window matters. At 36 months the tangency portfolio is also last,
`r sprintf("%.2f", at_w(36, "gap"))` of Sharpe ratio behind the best rule that
estimates no mean; at 120 months it ranks `r at_w(120, "rank_tan")` of
`r nrow(reg)` and the gap is `r sprintf("%.2f", at_w(120, "gap"))`.

The claim the book carries out of this table is the one that holds at every
window: the rules that estimate no mean are ahead of the rule that estimates
one, and the gap closes as the estimation window lengthens, which is what a
sampling error in the mean that shrinks with $W$ predicts. Neither part is a
surprise to the literature: @demiguel2009 find, across fourteen rules and seven
datasets, that no mean-based rule consistently outperforms equal weighting, and
@jagannathan2003 report the strength of minimum variance. What this table adds
is that it happens on a market whose covariance structure can be inspected and
with a solver whose failures have been counted.

### A backtest is a measurement, and it has an error bar

The Sharpe ratios above are point estimates from `r Tn` monthly observations
of @eq-25-backtest. Under independent and identically distributed returns,
@lo2002 gives the asymptotic standard error

$$
\operatorname{se}(\widehat{SR}) \approx
\sqrt{\frac{1 + \tfrac{1}{2}SR^2}{T}} ,
$$ {#eq-25-se}

which, applied to the monthly Sharpe ratio over `r Tn` months and annualized,
works out as follows.

```{r}
#| label: error-bar
sr <- reg |>
  dplyr::select(strategy, sharpe) |>
  dplyr::mutate(se = sqrt((1 + (sharpe / sqrt(12))^2 / 2) / Tn) * sqrt(12),
                lower = sharpe - 1.96 * se,
                upper = sharpe + 1.96 * se)
sr
stopifnot(all(outer(sr$lower, sr$upper, `<=`)))   # every interval overlaps every other
```

Every interval overlaps every other. On this sample none of the differences
between these five strategies is statistically distinguishable from zero,
including the gap between the best and the worst.

Two caveats point in opposite directions. @eq-25-se assumes independent and
identically distributed returns, which @sec-04-descriptive-analysis-application
showed this market violates, so the true intervals are if anything wider;
@ledoit2008 give a bootstrap procedure that does not need the assumption, and
@jobson1981 with the correction of @memmel2003 give the test for a difference
between two Sharpe ratios rather than for each separately. Against that, these
five strategies were not selected from a large search, so the multiple-testing
correction of @white2000 and @sullivan1999, and the deflated Sharpe ratio of
@bailey2014, would not widen them much further. A study that had tried a hundred
specifications would need all of that machinery.

The honest reading does not undo the chapter, because two things survive it. The
turnover and cost differences are not estimates but arithmetic on observed trades,
and they are large. The failure count is not an estimate either: a strategy
infeasible in `r length(fail)` months of one year has a property no confidence
interval averages away.

The conclusions worth keeping are the ones that do not depend on the third decimal
of a Sharpe ratio. Most of the useful ones do not.

Two later chapters take this further rather than repeating it.
@sec-26-forecast-error-cost-theory asks what forecast error costs in Sharpe
ratio directly, instead of inferring it from a table of outcomes, and
@sec-28-robustness-theory asks what to do when the model itself is in doubt
rather than only its parameters.

### Attribution: where the return came from

A backtest says what a strategy earned. Attribution says which decisions earned
it, and the standard decomposition is @brinson1986 and @brinson1991. Writing
$w_i$ and $b_i$ for the portfolio and benchmark weights in segment $i$, and $r_i$
and $\beta_i$ for the segment returns,

$$
\underbrace{\sum_i (w_i - b_i)\beta_i}_{\text{allocation}}
+ \underbrace{\sum_i b_i (r_i - \beta_i)}_{\text{selection}}
+ \underbrace{\sum_i (w_i - b_i)(r_i - \beta_i)}_{\text{interaction}}
= \sum_i w_i r_i - \sum_i b_i \beta_i .
$$ {#eq-25-brinson}

The three terms separate the decision to overweight a segment from the decision
of what to hold inside it. For this book that split is the one the part structure
is built on: allocation is Parts IV and V, selection is Part VI, and
@eq-25-brinson is what tells an investor afterwards which of the two was worth
paying for.

The raw material is already available. `Return.portfolio(verbose = TRUE)` returns
per-asset contributions for every period, as @sec-23-rebalancing-implementation
showed, and those contributions are the $w_i r_i$ terms of @eq-25-brinson.
@sec-24-benchmarks-and-active-risk-theory does the work.

One caution about the famous result. @brinson1986 is routinely cited for the
claim that asset allocation explains about ninety percent of performance, and
@ibbotson2000 show that the number answers a different question from the one it
is usually quoted for: it is the share of the variance of returns *over time* for
a single fund, not the share of the difference *between* funds, which is far
smaller. Both are worth knowing, and conflating them is the most common misuse of
an attribution result in the industry.

### A taxonomy of look-ahead

@eq-25-backtest is defined so that $\hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_t$ sees only data before
$t$. Violations of that rule are the most common defect in a backtest and they
are rarely as obvious as using next month's return. Four kinds recur.

The estimation window can be misaligned, using data through $t$ rather than
$t-1$. The one-period lag in the market proxy of
@sec-05-factor-models-implementation exists for exactly this reason.

The universe can be chosen with hindsight. Every asset in this book's modeled
market survives to the end of the sample, which is a survivorship bias by
construction and one the real data sleeves of @sec-02-notation-and-data-real-data do not
share.

Parameters can be tuned on the same sample they are scored on. An estimation
window length, a shrinkage intensity, a rebalancing frequency: each is a choice,
and choosing it by looking at the out-of-sample result makes that result in-sample
[@harvey2015]. The sweep behind @tbl-25-register reports all nine configurations
rather than the best one for this reason.

Vendor data can be revised after the fact. Macroeconomic series in particular are
restated for years, so a backtest using the current vintage uses numbers nobody
had at the time.

Only the first is a coding error. The other three are design decisions, and
@lo2004 makes the broader point that a rule fitted to one regime and tested on
the same history is measuring the regime rather than the rule.

## Key Takeaways {.unnumbered}

- A backtest is @eq-25-backtest: an estimate produced by a rule that may see only
  the past. Every statistic computed from it carries a standard error
  [@harvey2015].
- `rolling_window` is inclusive at both ends, so asking for 60 gives 61
  observations. Almost no published result says which convention it used.
- `optimize.portfolio.rebalancing()` stores a failed period in the result list,
  as a portfolio of `NA` weights when `ROI` reports no solution and as a
  condition object when a solver throws, and completes normally. The object has
  the right class, the right length and the right names.
- The failures are not random. All `r length(fail)` here fall within one year,
  at the end of the equity bear market and just after it, which is precisely the
  stretch in which the mandate was impossible. Dropping them reports the average
  of the easy months.
- Always diagnose every period and always carry the failure count into the result
  table. A backtest with `r length(fail)` failures is a different object from
  one with none.
- The rebalancing loop contains `%dopar%` but registers no backend, so it runs on
  one core and says so in a warning that reads like noise. Registering eight
  workers cut 273 seconds to 61 with identical results.
- Applying @eq-25-se to the register, every confidence interval overlaps every
  other. The differences in turnover, in cost, and in feasibility are not
  estimates and do not overlap.

## Exercises {.unnumbered}

1. Rerun the mandate backtest with `return_target` at 0.002 and 0.005 monthly.
   Report the number of failed periods in each and when they occur. At which
   target does the strategy stop being a strategy?
2. Replace `rolling_window = win - 1L` with `rolling_window = win` and confirm
   that the windows now hold sixty-one observations. How much does the Sharpe
   ratio of the minimum-variance strategy move?
3. Run the same backtest with an expanding window (`rolling_window = NULL`).
   Does it do better or worse, and is the difference larger than the error bar
   computed above?
4. Take the failed periods and ask what a manager would actually have done. Implement one answer, rerun, and say plainly how your version differs
   from the strategy that was specified.
